ethiopia.title: 'Stop Arming Ethiopia's Enemies' - Abiy Tells Eritrea, Says Addis Abeba Seeks Red Sea Access Through Dialogue
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: 'Stop Arming Ethiopia's Enemies' - Abiy Tells Eritrea, Says Addis Abeba Seeks Red Sea Access Through Dialogue - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: 'Stop Arming Ethiopia's Enemies' - Abiy Tells Eritrea, Says Addis Abeba Seeks Red Sea Access Through Dialogue 26 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has called on the Eritrean government to "stop arming" and supporting forces opposed to Ethiopia, warning that continued cooperation with what he described as Ethiopia's enemies would undermine prospects for peaceful relations between the two neighboring countries. Addressing the House of Peoples' Representatives (HoPR) during its fourth regular session of the first working year of the 7th Parliament, Abiy said Ethiopia wanted peaceful coexistence and shared development with Eritrea but expected Asmara to end its alleged support for armed groups operating against the Ethiopian government. "What do we want from the Eritrean government? Two things. First, stop arming Ethiopia's enemies, being a supply line, and cooperating with Ethiopia's enemies. Second, let us work together for shared development in every sphere," Abiy said. His remarks followed a question from MP Dagnew Lakew, who accused the Eritrean government of pursuing a longstanding destructive policy toward Ethiopia and supporting internal forces seeking to undermine the country's peace and stability. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Dagnew asked how long the government would tolerate what he characterized as Eritrea's repeated hostile actions, urging Abiy to clarify the administration's response and its practical measures to protect Ethiopia's security. Abiy said his government had repeatedly sought cooperation with Eritrea, including proposals to extend electricity supplies, construct roads and jointly develop port infrastructure. He claimed these initiatives had been rejected by the Eritrean government. "We have made high efforts with the Eritrean government to develop together," he said, adding that Ethiopia had offered to extend electricity infrastructure at its own expense and supply power to Eritrea at domestic Ethiopian prices. The prime minister also revisited Eritrea's involvement in the Tigray war, acknowledging what he described as "positive initial conduct" when Ethiopian troops retreated toward Eritrea following the attack on the Northern Command. He said Eritrean authorities had received the troops without disarming them, provided water and held them until they could reorganize. However, he accused Eritrean forces of subsequently killing civilians and looting factories, schools and other property in Tigray as the war deepened. "We thank them, yet do not harm our people; our people are ultimately our own people, and we do not want them harmed improperly," he said. Abiy further alleged that Eritrean forces withdrew from Tigray following the Pretoria Agreement but that resources taken from the region were transported into Eritrea. Red Sea ambitions and regional security On securing access to the Red Sea, Abiy rejected claims that the country intended to invade Eritrea, insisting that Addis Abeba wanted to pursue its maritime interests through peaceful negotiations. "Now they say, 'Ethiopia is going to invade Eritrea, Ethiopia will wage an invasion for the Red Sea' - we will not wage an invasion. Invasion is not needed; we want it peacefully and through dialogue," he said. He nevertheless described Ethiopia's renewed attention to the Red Sea as a strategic awakening, arguing that previous Ethiopian political leaders had failed to adequately recognize the country's enduring maritime interests. "One thing we must recognize is that there was drift; at some point in time, Ethiopia's political elite erred in its awareness regarding the Red Sea. Now we are in a strategic awakening," Abiy said. He argued that Ethiopia's security and economic stability were inseparable from the stability of the wider Horn of Africa, given its population, geographical size and regional influence. "Because we are a large tree, if we stand firm our shade reaches the neighborhood, yet if our trunk is harmed, everyone is harmed," he said. Abiy also argued that the Red Sea's geopolitical significance could change in the coming years as emerging maritime routes, particularly the Northern Sea Route through the Arctic, reshape international trade. He cited Russian investment in icebreakers and the gradual opening of Arctic shipping routes as developments that could challenge the Red Sea's historical position as a major trade corridor connecting Asia and Europe. He suggested that the region's current geopolitical tensions should be understood against these changing international trade and security dynamics. The prime minister also defended Ethiopia's acquisition of advanced military capabilities, including Su-35 fighter aircraft, saying the country's military modernization was intended to deter aggression rather than threaten neighboring states. "What we have armed ourselves with is to defend Ethiopia and the region from the volatile situation now visible. We have no desire to attack anyone," he said. He added that the development of long-range strike capabilities had become increasingly important because such capabilities were no longer exclusive to states, with armed groups and terrorist organizations also able to launch attacks over considerable distances. "No one - whether small or big - can cross into Ethiopia's border, invade Ethiopia, and return in honor," Abiy warned, invoking the historic Battle of Adwa as a symbol of Ethiopia's determination to defend its sovereignty. Military modernization and regional role Abiy said the government was pursuing a broader military modernization strategy built around technological advancement, domestic manufacturing, training and institutional self-reliance. He said the Ministry of Defense had made progress in producing military uniforms, food supplies and ammunition domestically, contrasting this with the country's dependence on foreign suppliers during the first Tigray war. He also claimed that Ethiopia had exported military products worth hundreds of millions of dollars in the previous year, including ammunition, drones and aircraft maintenance services. The prime minister said the Ethiopian National Defense Force was being developed not only to defend the country's sovereignty but also to anticipate geopolitical threats, deter conflict and support regional stability. He described Ethiopia as an established contributor to regional and international peacekeeping, citing its historical military deployments in Korea, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Liberia, Sudan and Somalia. "The institution is not being built for Ethiopia alone. Our region is fragile; for our region we are an older brother," he said. His remarks come amid heightened regional sensitivities surrounding Ethiopia's pursuit of Red Sea access, its military modernization and increasingly strained relations with Eritrea. Armed groups and Ethiopia's internal security On domestic security, Abiy acknowledged continuing insecurity in parts of the country but argued that armed groups operating in Oromia, Amhara and Tigray were undermining civilian safety and regional stability. He characterized these groups as an internal threat, using the analogy of an "autoimmune disease" to describe forces he accused of attacking their own communities and fighting among themselves while claiming to represent ethnic or political interests. "One autoimmune disease is in Oromia," he said, alleging that armed groups were attacking civilians and disrupting daily life. He made similar accusations against armed groups operating in Amhara and Tigray, arguing that their activities were harming farmers, women, teachers and students. Abiy also accused some armed groups of shifting from ethnic-based mobilization to religious narratives to sustain their influence, warning that attempts to exploit religious differences would not succeed. He called on armed groups in the three regions to abandon violence and enter peaceful negotiations with the government. "My advice and call is that it is better to enter peacefully and work peacefully," he said, citing previous government engagements with armed groups, including the Pretoria Agreement with the TPLF and the unconditional invitation extended to armed opposition groups following the 2018 political reform. The prime minister said thousands of armed fighters were entering the government's fold across different regions, arguing that dialogue remained the preferred approach for resolving internal conflicts. He also acknowledged that security forces alone could not guarantee safety throughout Ethiopia, calling for stronger cooperation between communities and security institutions, particularly through information sharing and local protection mechanisms. Responding to concerns over continued violence in Arsi and other parts of Oromia, Abiy said police officers and local militia members had been killed while attempting to protect civilians. He cited leadership changes, public consultations and efforts to strengthen local self-protection as part of the government's response. He urged parliamentarians and political actors to condemn attacks against civilians regardless of who perpetrated them, arguing that politicizing security incidents weakened collective efforts to address the violence. Tigray and the path to political normalization On Tigray, Abiy said the government's priority was to consolidate peace, restore basic services and facilitate the region's return to normal political and administrative life. He listed the restoration of air transport, telephone services, banking and fuel supplies, the resumption of government services and preparations for elections as key priorities. He said the government intended to ensure that Tigray's residents could elect their own representatives and administer the region through a peaceful political process. "Our primary task is to establish complete peace in Tigray, restore basic services ... hold a swift election so that the right of the Tigray people, who fought for long years to administer themselves, is respected," he said. Abiy also criticized what he described as continued resistance by some Tigrayan political leaders to the post-war political process, accusing them prolonging confrontation at the expense of the population. He said some leaders had treated continued militancy and confrontation as a form of heroism while sacrificing Tigrayan youth to maintain their political relevance. "People emerged there who thought constant militancy, constant confrontation, and constant signs of contradiction were heroism, sacrificing Tigray's youth to a high degree to prolong their own relevance," he said. He urged Tigrayan political elites to abandon what he characterized as the old confrontational approach, support peaceful elections and allow the region's residents to choose their own leadership. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has urged Eritrea to cease its support for armed groups opposing Ethiopia, warning that such actions jeopardize peaceful relations between the two nations. Speaking to the House of Peoples' Representatives, Abiy emphasized Ethiopia's desire for cooperation and shared development with Eritrea, while calling for an end to Eritrea's alleged military assistance to Ethiopia's enemies. He highlighted Ethiopia's efforts to engage Eritrea in joint projects, including infrastructure development, which have been rejected by Asmara. Abiy also addressed Ethiopia's strategic interests in accessing the Red Sea, asserting that the country seeks peaceful negotiations rather than military confrontation. Additionally, he acknowledged ongoing internal security challenges posed by armed groups in various regions, advocating for dialogue and cooperation to resolve conflicts. Abiy reaffirmed the government's commitment to restoring peace and services in Tigray and criticized certain Tigrayan leaders for prolonging unrest at the expense of the population.

Opinion November 26, 2026 Updated: November 26, 2026 Ethiopia’s Deteriorating Human Rights and Security Crisis: A Call for Stronger U.S. Diplomatic Leadership November 26, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Google Map by Mesfin Mekonen The situation on the ground in Ethiopia, particularly in the Arsi region of Oromia, continues to deteriorate, with reports of ongoing killings, abductions, and attacks against innocent civilians. The continued violence and the apparent failure to provide adequate protection for vulnerable communities are deeply troubling. The reported killings of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, along with the burning and destruction of their homes, churches, and properties, are particularly alarming. These horrific incidents have caused profound suffering among affected communities and have raised serious concerns among Ethiopian Americans and peace-loving people around the world. The continued targeting of civilians and religious communities must not be allowed to escalate further. Ethiopia is already experiencing serious instability across multiple regions. If these atrocities and security threats are not addressed promptly and decisively, there is a real danger that the violence could spread, intensify, and become increasingly difficult to contain. We are also deeply concerned about reports of terrorist networks operating in the region and their alleged connections with Al-Shabaab, as well as the broader deterioration of security, human rights, and humanitarian conditions throughout Ethiopia. These concerns require serious attention, credible investigation, and coordinated regional and international engagement. Ethiopian Americans’ Disappointment with U.S. Diplomatic Leadership Ethiopian Americans are deeply disappointed with Ambassador Massinga’s handling of the deteriorating human rights and humanitarian situation in Ethiopia, particularly what many regard as the absence of a sufficiently strong and unequivocal public statement condemning the horrific killings of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians in the Arsi region of Oromia and the destruction of their homes, churches, and properties. At a time when innocent civilians are being targeted, religious communities are facing growing threats, and serious human rights violations continue, the United States must demonstrate clear, principled, and consistent diplomatic leadership. We expect the U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia to uphold American values, defend religious freedom, speak forcefully against atrocities, and advocate for the protection of all innocent civilians, regardless of their ethnicity, religion, or political affiliation. Unfortunately, Ambassador Massinga’s response has fallen short of the expectations of many Ethiopian Americans who look to the United States for principled leadership and meaningful engagement. Effective American diplomacy requires more than maintaining diplomatic relations. It demands courage, impartiality, accountability, and a willingness to address serious human rights violations directly and transparently. The United States has an important role to play in encouraging the Ethiopian government to fulfill its fundamental responsibility to protect its citizens and ensure that perpetrators of violence are held accountable. A Call for Stronger U.S. Engagement and Regional Diplomacy As Ethiopian American advocates, we respectfully urge the U.S. Congress and the Administration to consider the following priorities: 1. Appoint a Senior Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa The Administration should consider appointing and empowering a senior-level Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa with the authority, experience, and diplomatic resources necessary to address the growing regional crisis. The Special Envoy should engage directly with the leadership of Ethiopia and Eritrea and coordinate diplomatic initiatives with the African Union (AU), the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), and the United Nations. A high-level diplomatic representative could play a critical role in coordinating regional engagement, preventing further conflict, reducing tensions, and facilitating meaningful negotiations toward lasting peace and stability. We believe this position should be filled by a highly capable, experienced, and proactive career diplomat with a strong understanding of the political, security, and humanitarian challenges facing the Horn of Africa. Such an individual must be prepared to engage all relevant stakeholders, advance U.S. foreign policy interests, and demonstrate the strong diplomatic leadership that this critical moment demands. 2. Prioritize the Protection of Innocent Civilians The United States should make the protection of civilians a central priority in its engagement with the Ethiopian government and other relevant stakeholders. This includes urging authorities to take immediate and effective measures to prevent further killings, abductions, religious persecution, and the destruction of civilian property. All communities must be protected equally, without discrimination based on ethnicity, religion, or political affiliation. 3. Defend Religious Freedom and Condemn Attacks on Religious Communities The United States should publicly and unequivocally condemn attacks against Ethiopian Orthodox Christians and other religious communities. Religious freedom is a fundamental human right, and attacks on churches, clergy, worshippers, and religious institutions must not be ignored or treated as ordinary security incidents. Credible allegations of religiously motivated violence should be investigated independently, and those responsible must be held accountable. 4. Support Accountability and Human Rights Investigations The U.S. Congress and the Administration should encourage credible, independent investigations into reported atrocities, including the killings of civilians and the destruction of religious institutions and civilian property. Accountability is essential to preventing further violence, restoring public confidence, and ensuring that victims and their families receive justice. 5. Promote an Inclusive and Sustainable Peace Process Ethiopia’s continuing conflicts cannot be resolved through military force alone. A sustainable solution requires inclusive dialogue, meaningful political engagement, and the participation of all relevant stakeholders. The United States should use its diplomatic influence to encourage a genuine, inclusive peace process that addresses the root causes of conflict and supports national reconciliation, constitutional reform, democratic governance, and respect for human rights. Conclusion: The United States Must Not Remain Silent The United States must not remain silent or appear indifferent when innocent civilians are being killed, religious communities are under attack, and the security and humanitarian situation in Ethiopia continues to deteriorate. Ethiopian Americans are deeply concerned about the future of Ethiopia and the potential consequences of continued violence and instability for the entire Horn of Africa. We respectfully urge Congress and the Administration to demonstrate stronger, more consistent, and more effective diplomatic leadership. The time for meaningful engagement is now. The protection of innocent civilians, the defense of religious freedom, the promotion of justice and accountability, and the pursuit of lasting peace must remain at the center of U.S. policy toward Ethiopia. Ethiopian Americans deserve to see American diplomacy reflect the fundamental principles of human rights, religious freedom, justice, and accountability. The international community must act before the crisis escalates further. The cost of continued silence and inaction could be devastating—not only for Ethiopia, but for the stability and security of the entire Horn of Africa. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia’s Calculated Use of Maritime Diplomacy to Camouflage its Irredentist Ambitions in the Region - Eritrea Ministry Of Information
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Calculated Use of Maritime Diplomacy to Camouflage its Irredentist Ambitions in the Region – Eritrea Ministry Of Information Business is booming. Likes Followers Subscribers Followers Likes Followers Subscribers Followers Friday, November 27, 2026 Home Articles Nation Building Q & A General Arts & Sports About Eritrea History & Culture Today in History Eritrea at a Glance Erina Proverbs Press Release Editorial Newspapers Haddas Ertra Eritrea Alhaditha Eritrea Haddas Eritrea Profile Magazines Men’esey Magazine Shebab Magazine Agizo Magazine Men’esey Magazine (Arabic) Contact us Publisher - Home Articles Nation Building Q & A General Arts & Sports About Eritrea History & Culture Today in History Eritrea at a Glance Erina Proverbs Press Release Editorial Newspapers Haddas Ertra Eritrea Alhaditha Eritrea Haddas Eritrea Profile Magazines Men’esey Magazine Shebab Magazine Agizo Magazine Men’esey Magazine (Arabic) Contact us Home Articles General Ethiopia’s Calculated Use of Maritime Diplomacy to Camouflage its Irredentist Ambitions in the Region Ethiopia’s Calculated Use of Maritime Diplomacy to Camouflage its Irredentist Ambitions in the Region General Last updated Nov 26, 2026 Share The onus rests squarely on the international community to look beyond Ethiopia’s carefully choreographed diplomatic rhetoric and judge its intentions by the explicit pronouncements and actions of its political and military establishment. Whenever the Ethiopian ruling party finds itself bereft of a defensible legal argument for an array of warped and unlawful ambitions in the region, its customary reflex is to convene a symposium. Over the past year, consistent with its three-year campaign of aggression against the State of Eritrea, the Prosperity Party (PP), in predictable fashion, has embarked on a convoluted campaign of maritime forum diplomacy. Through the Organisation of blue-economy conferences, the dispatch of delegations to naval security panels, and the sponsorship of strategic dialogues, the Ethiopian regime has sought to manufacture a veneer of international legitimacy around its illegal demand for “sovereign sea access,” in the futile effort to launder territorial revisionism through multilateral engagement. In diplomacy, form invariably betrays intent. Consider the conceptual paradox witnessed in late October 2026, when the Ethiopian Navy, a military institution belonging to a landlocked country, presided over a European Union-supported workshop on maritime security and search-and-rescue operations that brought together Naval Representatives from Puntland and Somaliland alongside the Representatives from Djibouti. By assembling select, non-autonomous, coastal actors while pointedly bypassing the Federal Government of Somalia in favor of regional administrations, the organizers inadvertently exposed the underlying political architecture of the exercise. A genuinely technical workshop on navigational safety does not begin by undermining the recognized sovereignty of a coastal state. Rather, such platforms appear designed to normalize the participation of a landlocked state in Red Sea security arrangements, gradually eroding the fundamental legal and geographical distinction between littoral states and their hinterland neighbours. This institutional choreography is further reinforced through domestic policy platforms, such as the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, and newly established strategic institutes, where state-aligned interlocutors routinely advance a doctrine that should alarm the international community. Notably, the recent Tana High-Level Forum, convened in of Bahir Dar from 23–25 October 2026, served as yet another platform to project this dangerous agenda. Addressing the forum, Ethiopia’s National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) Director General, Ambassador Redwan Hussein, argued that because the Red Sea has evolved into a geopolitical nexus for global superpowers, driven by its strategic significance, abundant resources, and critical commercial arteries, landlocked-Ethiopia insists on being granted a formal role in guaranteeing its maritime security. He maintained that the responsibility of securing the Red Sea is not a mandate reserved solely for coastal nations. Stripped of its academic varnish, the PP’s distorted proposition is that Ethiopia’s demographic scale, reportedly exceeding 130 million, and its mounting macroeconomic pressures, somehow confer a quasi-moral entitlement to override the established territorial boundaries of neighbouring states. PP officials routinely speak of refusing to remain a “prisoner of geography” and portray Ethiopia’s return to the Red Sea as a “historical inevitability”. Yet invoking demographic weight or economic necessity to justify claims over another nation’s coastline is neither legitimate nor given; it is a familiar rhetoric of irredentism. For Eritrea, the legal and historical record admits no ambiguity, nor does it require an endless succession of seminar rooms to amplify the indelible truth. International law establishes a clear and well-established equilibrium between the sovereign rights of coastal states and the transit needs of landlocked countries. Landlocked states enjoy the right of access to and from the sea through good-faith negotiated commercial arrangements, governed by applicable international law, appropriate bilateral agreements, and the sovereign regulatory jurisdiction of transit states. What international law does not confer upon them, however, is any unilateral entitlement to annex port infrastructure, station naval assets on foreign shores, or impose arrangements that compromise the sovereignty of a neighbouring coastal state. Moreover, Eritrea has never opposed mutually beneficial commercial utilization of its ports, provided such arrangements are founded on respect for Eritrean sovereignty. Indeed, even following the outbreak of the Eritrea-Ethiopia border war in May 1998, Eritrea did not block or obstruct Ethiopia’s access to its port facilities at Assab and Massawa. Eritrea’s subsequent offers for Ethiopia to use its ports to facilitate the transportation of vital food assistance in 2000 and again in 2002 were likewise rejected by Ethiopia. In a stark reversal, the PP now weaponizes that self-inflicted isolation, framing “sovereign sea access” as an existential imperative to justify expansionist rhetoric and military aggression. Furthermore, following the 2018 peace declaration, Eritrea once again opened its doors in good faith, offering an opportunity to transcend the destructive legacy of confrontation and establish a new foundation for bilateral cooperation. It was the Ethiopian ruling party, however, that squandered this historic opportunity, reverting instead to hegemonic nostalgia, belligerent posturing, and increasingly brazen territorial rhetoric. This historical record exposes the hollowness of today’s narrative: Ethiopia’s lack of access to Eritrean ports was never the consequence of an Eritrean policy of exclusion, but rather a consequence of decisions taken by successive Ethiopian governments. The international community must therefore discern Ethiopia’s carefully designed diplomatic rhetoric and assess its intentions against the explicit pronouncements and conduct of its political and military establishment . Diplomacy is rendered meaningless when conciliatory language in conference halls and hotel ballrooms is simultaneously contradicted by the Army’s top brass and senior Government officials openly threatening to secure sea access through the use of force; designating Assab as a strategic objective; and questioning the inviolability of internationally recognized borders. A government, in this case of a landlocked country, cannot credibly posture as a guarantor of Red Sea maritime security while its own senior officials contemplate actions that would constitute a flagrant violation of Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter, which unequivocally prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. The increasingly brazen character of this irredentist rhetoric was further underscored on 13 November 2026, when Ethiopia’s Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, in an address to representatives of the city of Mekele, asserted that Dogali, Gundet, and Adulis belonged to Tigray, before extending this extraordinary historical revisionism to Somalia by claiming that the port of Zeila was originally Ethiopian. Such pronouncements are neither isolated verbal indiscretions nor inconsequential political theatrics. They are part and parcel of the ruling Prosperity Party’s longstanding and deeply troubling irredentist narrative, which seeks to manufacture historical pretexts for territorial claims against Eritrea and other countries in the Horn of Africa. The international community would be gravely mistaken to dismiss such declarations as mere domestic political posturing. When territorial pretensions are repeatedly articulated by senior military and political figures, particularly against the backdrop of explicit threats of force, they must be treated for what they are: a dangerous challenge to the sovereignty of neighbouring states, the inviolability of international borders, and the foundational principles of the international order. In the event, external partners, particularly European and multilateral donors providing financial or institutional backing to maritime initiatives involving landlocked states with publicly declared expansionist agenda, would do well to reflect on the wider implications and unintended consequences of their patronage. Subsidizing revisionist narratives does not advance regional integration or maritime security; it risks emboldening adventurism along one of the world’s most strategically sensitive maritime corridors. In contrast to the PP’s destabilizing ambiguity, Eritrea’s principled position on the Red Sea is straightforward and firmly anchored in regional consensus: the security, environmental stewardship, and governance of the Red Sea are the exclusive prerogatives of its littoral states. Non-littoral actors possess neither the geographical standing nor the sovereign mandate to dictate the security architecture governing the Red Sea. Admitting non-coastal states into mechanisms intended for littoral governance inevitably dilutes the sovereign prerogatives of coastal nations, invites extraneous great-power rivalries and proxy competition, and risks undermining the stability of international maritime trade. This principle was reaffirmed on 4 October 2026, when the leaders of Eritrea, Egypt, Somalia, and Sudan issued the El Alamein Joint Declaration , underscoring that, while freedom of navigation remains inviolable, the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive prerogative of its coastal states. Together, these littoral nations have articulated a clear position in defence of sovereignty, territorial integrity, and non-interference. Crucially, it must also be underscored that the wider Red Sea states, cognizant of the geostrategic and geopolitical significance of the corridor, are continuously engaged in structured diplomatic consultations. Reaffirming that Red Sea security rests squarely with its direct littoral states, these nations are engaged in accurately identifying threats to regional peace in order to better coordinate future security measures. Worth noting is Eritrea’s own track record: across 35 years of independence, its Red Sea coastline has recorded zero incidents of piracy or maritime insecurity. Meanwhile, major global powers, including the United States and China, continue to uphold the position that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Horn of Africa nations must be strictly respected, and that Red Sea security remains the exclusive domain of the concerned littoral states. Ultimately, any seasoned observer of the Horn of Africa would recognize that the PP’s sudden preoccupation with maritime forums has far less to do with the technical imperatives of trade logistics than with domestic political survival and the calculated use of maritime rhetoric to camouflage its irredentist ambitions in the region. Confronted with protracted internal conflicts, acute economic dislocation, and deepening fractures within its internal governance architecture, Ethiopia’s ruling establishment appears increasingly inclined to manufacture an external strategic preoccupation to rally domestic sentiment and divert attention from its mounting governance failures. Yet the modern history of the region offers an unmistakable lesson: successive Ethiopian administrations that have sought to resolve their internal political crises by projecting instability beyond their borders have invariably ended up compounding their own vulnerabilities and courting strategic ruin. Sovereignty, at the end of the day, is not an obsolete artifact to be negotiated away in policy colloquiums, and internationally recognized boundaries are not provisional suggestions. Eritrea remains steadfast in its commitment to genuine regional peace, mutually beneficial economic cooperation, and respect for international law. But it will not surrender an inch of its territory or maritime domain to diplomatic theatre, economic coercion, or the threat or use of force. The Eritrean Ministry of Information argues that Ethiopia's Prosperity Party (PP) is using international forums to legitimize its claims for "sovereign sea access," despite being a landlocked nation. This includes hosting maritime security workshops while bypassing the recognized sovereignty of Somalia. The PP's rhetoric suggests a belief that Ethiopia's large population and economic pressures justify territorial expansion, which Eritrea firmly contests. Eritrea maintains that its ports are open for mutually beneficial use, provided its sovereignty is respected. The article warns that the international community must critically assess Ethiopia's intentions, as its aggressive rhetoric poses a threat to regional stability and the principles of international law.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Rules Out Military Action Against Eritrea – Is a Different Breakthrough Possible? – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-26 Ethiopia Rules Out Military Action Against Eritrea – Is a Different Breakthrough Possible? 0 Comments Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has effectively ruled out military action against Eritrea in remarks to the new parliament, which began its term in October following elections held in June. The position holds even though Ethiopian troops now face their Eritrean counterparts along the border, after repelling a rebel attack in September that Eritrea supported directly and in which Eritrean soldiers themselves crossed into Ethiopia. According to the prime minister, Ethiopia’s posture towards Eritrea remains in essence what it was before the recent escalation, and it rests on two conditions. The first is cooperation with Eritrea on the “principles of give and take”, a reference to Ethiopia’s desire for access to the sea. The second concerns national security and requires Asmara to stop interfering in Ethiopia’s internal affairs, chiefly by ending its support for armed proxies. Both demands would require extensive reform and honest introspection from Isaias Afwerki’s regime. The present conundrum is itself the culmination of an escalatory trajectory taken up by Asmara, one that reflects a policy of antagonism and prickliness marking Eritrea’s relations chiefly with Ethiopia and, more or less consistently, with its other neighbours. Since seceding from Ethiopia in 1993, Eritrea might reasonably have approached its far more powerful and populous neighbour with good neighbourliness, aligning policies and interests for mutual benefit and regional integration. Asmara instead sought geopolitical weight, aiming to overpower Ethiopia and to dominate the Horn of Africa at large, shaping the politics of its neighbours along the way. The decision to go to war with Ethiopia in 1998, and to fight its other neighbours, Sudan, Djibouti and Yemen among them, embodied that quest. That strategy became the biggest factor in the isolated, militarised and harshly authoritarian structure that Eritrea eventually came to embody, that of a garrison state. The condition held from approximately 2001 until Ethiopia’s diplomatic push after Abiy took office in 2018, a fact he cited in his remarks to parliament. The rapprochement allowed Asmara to emerge from isolation and rekindle its ties across the Horn, yet reform never followed, according to Abiy, and Asmara’s entrenched foreign policy returned to the fore. It did not take long for Eritrea to become involved, militarily as well, in Ethiopia’s politics as well as in those of Sudan, which was undergoing upheaval of its own in 2019. Eritrea remains locked into the same combative foreign policy culture across its neighbourhood. Its involvement in Ethiopia’s internal politics has taken the form of mobilising Ethiopian rebel groups as proxies, and the foremost of them, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, has now, after Ethiopia’s battlefield victory inside Tigray, crossed into Eritrea and found safe haven there, as the prime minister himself has stated. Ethiopia’s position nonetheless signals a desire for a diplomatic solution to the standoff. It encourages the international community, chiefly those working to avert a war, to act to defuse tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which would mainly involve deterring the Eritrean government from its present course and encouraging it to enter dialogue with Addis Ababa. A diplomatic solution remains possible, yet the alternative of the two countries sliding into war would be costly. According to the prime minister, Ethiopia is guaranteed to emerge victorious, a claim that likely reflects the superior military capability Ethiopia has built up exponentially in recent years. That assurance sharpens the diplomatic imperative, for Eritrea more than for Ethiopia. In his address to the new parliament, Abiy emphasized Ethiopia's desire for diplomatic engagement, contingent on Eritrea's cooperation regarding two key issues: mutual benefits, particularly Ethiopia's access to the sea, and Eritrea ceasing its interference in Ethiopia's internal affairs. This stance reflects a broader historical context, where Eritrea's aggressive foreign policy has led to regional instability since its secession from Ethiopia in 1993. Abiy's remarks signal a push for international intervention to de-escalate tensions, highlighting the potential for dialogue over conflict. While Ethiopia's military capabilities have grown, the prime minister asserts that a peaceful resolution is preferable, underscoring the importance of reform within Eritrea to foster better relations. The situation remains delicate, with the risk of further conflict looming.

ethiopia.title: Two MPs Raise Alarm Over Civilian Killings, Displacement and Insecurity in Ethiopia During Abiy's Parliamentary Appearance
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Two MPs Raise Alarm Over Civilian Killings, Displacement and Insecurity in Ethiopia During Abiy's Parliamentary Appearance - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Two MPs Raise Alarm Over Civilian Killings, Displacement and Insecurity in Ethiopia During Abiy's Parliamentary Appearance 26 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Two Members of the House of Peoples' Representatives (HoPR) have raised concerns over escalating human rights violations, civilian killings and displacement in several parts of Ethiopia, questioning Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed about his government's response during a parliamentary session on Thursday. Abiy appeared before the House during the fourth regular session of the first working year of the 7th Parliament, where lawmakers are raising questions on a range of political, security and economic issues. The prime minister is responding to the concerns and questions raised by MPs. Dr. Aweke Hamzaye, an MP representing the Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA), said human rights violations had reached a deeply concerning level, citing findings by the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC). Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He said citizens' right to life remained precarious, with killings, maiming and looting attributed to government forces, locally operating armed groups, various factions and what he described as anti-peace elements. He warned that the violence had severely disrupted civilian life and threatened communities' existence. Aweke identified several affected areas, including parts of the Amhara region; Wollega, Arsi and Moyale in Oromia; Sodo and Abeshge in the Central Ethiopia region; and areas along the borders between the Koore and Burji zones of the South Ethiopia region and West Guji in Oromia. Focusing on the Koore community, the MP said residents had faced existential threats over the past 11 years due to repeated attacks by "extremist militants". He argued that despite repeated appeals to parliament and the federal government, the violence had continued, with attacks reported in recent days and at the time of his address. "Why has the government neglected this issue while this small population of Koore people has been continuously invaded and massacred for 11 consecutive years, putting their very existence at risk? What is the future hope and fate of these people?" he asked, urging the government to address what he described as an existential threat to the community and wider security challenges in the affected areas. Another MP, Gebremeskel Ademe of the Amhara Democratic Movement (ADM), questioned the government's handling of insecurity in Amhara, Oromia, Tigray and neighbouring areas, citing recurring killings and displacement in Arsi. He recalled what he described as a "horrific massacre" and displacement of civilians in Arsi in October 2026, saying repeated attacks had continued to leave residents seeking protection and assistance. "You should examine your government's structure in the area!" he told the prime minister, stressing that government legitimacy and public trust were essential to state-building. ethiopia.title: MP Urges Permanent 'Treason Law' Targeting Ethiopians Accused of Collaborating With Egypt
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: MP Urges Permanent 'Treason Law' Targeting Ethiopians Accused of Collaborating With Egypt - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: MP Urges Permanent 'Treason Law' Targeting Ethiopians Accused of Collaborating With Egypt 26 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — A member of Ethiopia's House of Peoples' Representatives has urged the government to introduce a permanent legal framework criminalizing Ethiopians accused of collaborating with Egypt to undermine the country's sovereignty, amid escalating regional tensions and growing diplomatic friction over Red Sea access. MP Kejela Merdassa made the proposal while questioning Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on regional peace and security, Ethiopia's quest for maritime access, and the activities of Egypt and Eritrea. He called on the executive to prepare legislation that could be submitted to parliament for approval, arguing that individuals who accept support or assignments from Egypt to destabilize Ethiopia should be held accountable for treason. "There must be a permanent legal framework that holds domestic traitors who collaborate with Egypt to attack Ethiopia accountable for the crime of treason," Kejela said. He accused Egypt of pursuing an undeclared war against Ethiopia, alleging that Cairo was seeking to prevent the country from securing its water rights, particularly over the Blue Nile, Baro-Akobo and Tekeze rivers, while also opposing Ethiopia's efforts to obtain access to the sea and the Red Sea. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Kejela alleged that domestic actors were receiving training, logistical, financial, security and moral support from Egypt to undermine Ethiopia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. He did not identify the individuals or groups he accused of collaborating with Egypt. The MP also questioned the government's progress in pursuing maritime access through what he described as a legal and natural process, asking what stage the effort had reached and what support parliament and other stakeholders were expected to provide. His remarks come as Ethiopia's pursuit of Red Sea access increasingly intersects with regional security tensions and diplomatic alignments. Egypt has intensified coordination with Eritrea and Sudan on Red Sea security and regional sovereignty, with trilateral talks held on November 21 and subsequent Egyptian-Sudanese discussions on reconstruction and opposing Red Sea militarization. The diplomatic coordination unfolds against renewed tensions along the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, where reports of military buildup and clashes near Badme in mid-November have heightened concerns over a possible inter-state escalation. The two countries' strained relations have also been shaped by competing regional security interests , allegations of support for armed actors, and Ethiopia's renewed push for sovereign maritime access. Kejela accused Egypt of waging an undeclared war against Ethiopia, particularly regarding water rights over the Blue Nile and other rivers, while also opposing Ethiopia's access to the Red Sea. His comments come amid rising tensions in the region, particularly between Ethiopia and Eritrea, and highlight concerns over security and diplomatic relations in the Horn of Africa. ethiopia.title: War in Amhara, Ethiopia, is Threatening Water Security in the Nile Basin - The Water Diplomat
ethiopia.content: War in Amhara, Ethiopia, is Threatening Water Security in the Nile Basin | The Water Diplomat Skip to Main Content Subscribe Hydropolitics News and Intelligence SEARCH SEARCH Subscribe Home About Us Newsletter Archive Contact Us Donations SEARCH War in Amhara, Ethiopia, is Threatening Water Security in the Nile Basin By Abebe Workneh, republished from Eurasia Review 26 Nov 2026 by The Water Diplomat A relentless war now entering its fourth year in Ethiopia's Amhara region is pushing the lifeblood of the Nile Basin to a breaking point. What began under a sweeping August 4, 2023 state of emergency—placing Amhara administration under military rule—has persisted even after the formal state of emergency period expired in June 2024 without further parliamentary extension, escalating into a sustained four-year campaign marked by combat drones (including Bayraktar TB2 and Wing Loong 2 models), heavy artillery, and MiG-23 and Su-27 fighter jets. Across four years of warfare, Ethiopian Orthodox Christian churches and monasteries—from Debre Elias in East Gojjam and monastic communities around Lake Tana to St. Arsema Monastery in South Wollo, struck on July 22, 2026—have repeatedly come under devastating drone attacks and heavy artillery bombardment by government forces, spreading death, destruction, and mass displacement across the very highlands that feed the Blue Nile. At the Source and Natural Reservoir of the Blue Nile Amhara stands as both the source and the natural reservoir of the Blue Nile—meaning an escalating war in Amhara threatens the water security of the entire Nile Basin. Winding roughly 800 kilometers (500 miles) across Amhara territory, the Blue Nile's headwaters rise in Gojjam a few miles from Lake Tana, fed by numerous tributaries that join before reaching the lake. Lake Tana acts as a vital natural reservoir regulating flow, while highland rains and tributary networks drive the river's surge downstream. When armed conflict tears through these headwaters and catchments, the shockwaves do not stop at Amhara's borders—they strike at the heart of the water lifeline sustaining Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. Choking Lake Tana and Creating a Basin-Wide Crisis Heavy military operations have shattered daily farming and stalled vital conservation across Amhara, leaving Lake Tana exposed to severe ecological degradation. Without active protection and stewardship, invasive water hyacinth threatens to surge unchecked, fouling water quality and choking native life just as military damage strains surrounding infrastructure (Ethiopian Human Rights Commission, 2024). Without a healthy Lake Tana, the Blue Nile faces profound disruption.“ Without Lake Tana, the Blue Nile is no more.” Because Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt depend on Nile waters for hydropower, agriculture, and survival, prolonged warfare in Amhara carries explosive regional stakes. Halted farming, abandoned climate adaptation efforts, and mounting ecological stress risk severe ecosystem damage and diminishing Blue Nile flow over time. With the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) now inaugurated and reliant in part on healthy upstream catchments in Amhara, continued instability threatens to inflame already volatile water disputes across the Nile Basin. Targeting Churches and Monasteries: Destroying Sacred Guardians of Ancient Forests Even more alarming, four years of relentless drone attacks and heavy artillery bombardment by government forces have turned Ethiopian Orthodox Christian churches and monasteries into primary targets of the war—imperiling the region's legendary "church forests," the sacred groves surrounding these sanctuaries that serve as living green islands across an otherwise deforested landscape. Documented incidents across Amhara show how historic religious centers along the Blue Nile watershed have repeatedly come under heavy fire: in East Gojjam, intense fighting and military assaults struck the ancient Debre Elias Monastery; in Wollo, heavy artillery encircled historic monastic centers such as Tedbabe Mariam, while a July 22, 2026 drone strike on Abbay Giyorgis St. Arsema Unity Monastery near Mekane Selam killed clergy and civilians and flattened monastic storehouses and water systems; and across the Lake Tana basin and Bahir Dar corridor, surrounding monastic communities and religious students have endured deadly raids, shelling, and siege conditions. As research on Ethiopian church forests shows, these sacred compounds act as irreplaceable living sanctuaries preserving ancient indigenous tree varieties that have vanished nearly everywhere else in the northern highlands. Protected for centuries by religious stewardship, these forest islands anchor hillside soils, safeguard springs, and regulate water runoff feeding Lake Tana and the Blue Nile's tributaries; when government drone strikes and heavy artillery shatter monastic and parish compounds year after year, they destroy centuries-old watershed guardians that cannot be replaced once burned or leveled. Diplomatic Blind Spots and Escalation Risks Treating the conflict in Amhara as a peripheral internal security issue creates a dangerous blind spot in regional diplomacy. Negotiations over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Red Sea security, and Horn of Africa stability often treat upstream water supply as a static backdrop rather than a system under active stress. Yet prolonged combat, displaced rural populations, and disrupted land and watershed management in Amhara directly affect sediment dynamics, seasonal runoff patterns, and local governance around the Blue Nile's headwaters. Ignoring the conflict does not insulate downstream states or international mediators from instability; instead, it leaves a core driver of regional water and security risk unaddressed while deepening grievances that fuel wider cycles of violence. What Credible De-Escalation Requires Raising the alarm is only a starting point unless international actors pair urgency with concrete mechanisms that protect civilians and watersheds simultaneously. Credible de-escalation requires an immediate halt to heavy weaponry and drone strikes affecting populated and sacred areas, independent human rights and humanitarian access, and an inclusive political process that brings Amhara stakeholders directly into talks rather than relying on exclusionary arrangements. Equally vital is safeguarding Lake Tana, its tributary catchments, and farming communities through verifiable local truces and environmental monitoring—recognizing that durable peace in Amhara and long-term water security across the Nile Basin are inseparable. Abebe Workneh is an economist and tax expert. He holds an MSc in Economic Development from the University of Houston and an MBA. His research on African economic integration, peace and security, and regional trade finance has appeared in several outlets, among them Eurasia Review and the International Journal of Diplomacy and Economy. ethiopia.summary: The ongoing war in Ethiopia's Amhara region, now in its fourth year, poses a significant threat to water security in the Nile Basin. Initiated under a military state of emergency in August 2023, the conflict has escalated, leading to devastating drone attacks and artillery bombardments on Ethiopian Orthodox Christian churches and monasteries, which are crucial for preserving the region's ecology. The Blue Nile, which originates in Amhara and is vital for Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt, is at risk due to the destruction of Lake Tana and its tributaries, essential for regulating water flow. The conflict has disrupted farming and conservation efforts, exacerbating ecological degradation and threatening the livelihoods of millions dependent on the Nile. Diplomatic efforts must address the conflict's implications for regional water security, emphasizing the need for immediate ceasefires, humanitarian access, and inclusive political dialogue to ensure both peace in Amhara and the long-term viability of the Nile Basin's water resources.

somalia.content: Somalia unveils new electronic passport in drive to regional integration - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia unveils new electronic passport in drive to regional integration Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Nuri Aden Friday November 27, 2026 Somalia has been working to modernise its travel documentation and strengthen immigration cooperation with member states of the East Africa Community bloc. Somalia's third-generation passport was unveiled at a meeting of East Africa's meeting immigration chiefs. / Others Somalia has presented its new third-generation electronic passport to East African Community (EAC) member states, marking another step towards regional integration and the modernisation of its immigration system. The passport was showcased during a three-day meeting of immigration chiefs in Kampala, Uganda, which concluded on Thursday. Somalia’s delegation was led by Hussein Qasim Yusuf, Director-General of the Immigration and Citizenship Agency, who briefed regional officials on the passport’s advanced security features and technology. advertisements The new travel document incorporates modern security measures while reflecting Somalia’s national identity, cultural heritage and traditions. The meeting focused on implementing EAC Council of Ministers’ decisions, harmonising immigration procedures and improving cooperation between member states. Officials also discussed the recognition of national identity cards, the modernisation of immigration services and measures to facilitate the movement of people across the region. EAC passport integration The presentation follows Somalia’s approval to adopt and issue the EAC electronic passport, a key requirement in the country’s efforts to align its travel documents with regional standards. In February 2026, Somalia’s Ambassador to Tanzania and Permanent Representative to the EAC, Ilyas Ali Hassan, formally handed over the authorisation to Somali Internal Security Minister Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail, known as Fartaag. The authorisation, granted in December 2025, allowed Somalia to adopt the EAC passport’s approved design and proceed with preparations for its issuance. Somalia has since been working to modernise its travel documentation and strengthen immigration cooperation with other member states. The EAC electronic passport was first launched during the bloc’s 17th Ordinary Heads of State Summit on 2 March 2016. It is issued in three categories: ordinary, service and diplomatic passports, replacing older national passports in participating countries. The document is designed to strengthen travel security, improve border management and facilitate regional mobility. Somalia officially joined the East African Community on 4 March 2024, becoming the regional bloc’s eighth member state. Since joining, Mogadishu has been working to align its policies and institutions with regional commitments, particularly in immigration, trade and the movement of people. The introduction of the electronic passport represents another step towards meeting those obligations and strengthening Somalia’s participation in the regional bloc. According to the latest Henley Passport Index, Somalia ranks 99th globally, with its passport providing access to 32 destinations without a prior visa. somalia.content: Türkiye inaugurates renovated school, breaks ground for hospital expansion in Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Türkiye inaugurates renovated school, breaks ground for hospital expansion in Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Mohamed Dhaysane Friday November 27, 2026 Projects mark latest phase of Türkiye’s support for Somalia’s education and health care sectors, Turkish Embassy says Türkiye has inaugurated a renovated school and laid the foundation stone for a hospital expansion in Warsheikh, in Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region, the Turkish Embassy in Mogadishu said Thursday. The ceremony included the inauguration of a renovated primary and secondary school in Warsheikh and the launch of a major hospital rehabilitation and expansion project, marking the latest phase of Türkiye’s support for Somalia’s education and health care sectors, the embassy said in a statement. advertisements The Turkish Embassy said the projects were implemented in cooperation with Türkiye’s Defense Ministry, the Somali Turkish Task Force Command and Albayrak Group. “This aimed at expanding healthcare services for residents of the district and surrounding communities”, the Turkish embassy in Somalia said. The developments came days after Türkiye broke ground in Mogadishu for the new headquarters of the Somali Naval Forces, a Joint Operations Center and related facilities. The groundbreaking took place during a visit to Somalia by Turkish Chief of General Staff Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu, who was hosted by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud at the presidential palace in Mogadishu on Saturday. Türkiye is one of Somalia’s closest security partners, and bilateral ties have deepened since Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan visited Somalia in 2011, when he was prime minister. Türkiye’s military training mission in Somalia, known as TURKSOM, has supported the country’s counterterrorism operations by providing military training and logistical support to Somali security forces in their fight against terrorist groups such as al-Shabaab and Daesh. somalia.title: Saadaq Joon replaces Ahmed Moallim Fiqi as Somalia's defence minister - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Saadaq Joon replaces Ahmed Moallim Fiqi as Somalia's defence minister - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Saadaq Joon replaces Ahmed Moallim Fiqi as Somalia's defence minister Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday November 23, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre appointed lawmaker Saadaq Omar Mohamed Hassan, widely known as Saadaq Joon, as the country's new defence minister on Monday, replacing Ahmed Moallim Fiqi in a limited Cabinet reshuffle that also affected two deputy ministers. In a decree issued Nov. 23, the Prime Minister's Office announced that Saadaq Joon would take over the Defence Ministry following Fiqi's departure from the position. advertisements The government did not specify why Fiqi left the ministry or announce whether he would be assigned another Cabinet position. Saadaq Joon, a member of Somalia's House of the People, previously served as commander of the Banadir Regional Police Force and has held several senior security positions. His appointment comes a day after Galmudug President Liibaan Ahmed Hassan announced a new regional Cabinet, following political changes in the central Somali state. According to political sources, Saadaq Joon's appointment is linked to a power-sharing arrangement between the federal government and former Galmudug President Ahmed Abdi Kaariye Qoorqoor following the election of Liibaan Ahmed Hassan. The reported arrangement is understood to involve the redistribution of senior government positions following the Galmudug leadership transition. However, the Prime Minister's Office did not publicly confirm that the defence appointment was part of a political agreement with Qoorqoor. The reshuffle also involved changes to two deputy ministerial positions. Ali Ifiye Ali was appointed deputy minister of ports and maritime transport, while Maryan Ali Abukar was named deputy minister of fisheries and the blue economy. The prime minister instructed the newly appointed officials to assume their responsibilities immediately and urged them to carry out their duties with integrity, dedication and accountability. Saadaq Joon takes over the Defence Ministry as Somalia continues military operations against al-Shabab and prepares to assume greater security responsibilities from African Union peacekeeping forces. The appointment also comes as the federal government and international partners discuss the future of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), whose current United Nations authorization expires Dec. 31. Fiqi had served as defence minister since April 2025, overseeing military operations against al-Shabab and cooperation with international security partners. somalia.content: Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 24, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni have called for intensified military operations against al-Shabab and alternative funding arrangements to sustain Ugandan troops deployed in Somalia, as uncertainty grows over the future of African Union peacekeeping operations. In a joint communiqué issued Monday, Nov. 23, following talks in Entebbe, Uganda, the two leaders emphasized the need for adequate, predictable and sustainable funding for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) and closer military cooperation to combat the al-Qaeda-linked militant group. advertisements The discussions came during Hassan Sheikh's one-day official visit to Uganda at Museveni's invitation, as Kampala begins a phased withdrawal of troops deployed under bilateral security arrangements with Somalia. The two presidents called on AUSSOM and the Somali National Armed Forces to increase offensive operations against al-Shabab while exploring alternative financing mechanisms for forces operating under bilateral agreements. They also urged closer coordination among countries contributing troops to the African Union mission to strengthen counterterrorism operations and preserve security gains achieved over nearly two decades. The leaders praised the contributions of the Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF), Somali troops and other African Union peacekeepers, paying tribute to soldiers killed or wounded during operations against al-Shabab. They reaffirmed their commitment to consolidating security gains achieved under AUSSOM and its predecessor missions, the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) and the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM). The presidents also referred to decisions reached during an extraordinary summit of AUSSOM troop-contributing countries held in Kampala on July 31, where leaders called for a coordinated security transition and sustained international financial assistance. Uganda, one of the largest contributors to African Union military operations in Somalia since 2007, began withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral arrangements earlier this month. The Ugandan military has also announced plans for a gradual withdrawal of its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027, raising concerns about potential security gaps in areas previously protected by its forces. However, Monday's communiqué did not announce any changes to Uganda's withdrawal timetable or confirm whether additional funding had been secured. Beyond military cooperation, Hassan Sheikh and Museveni emphasized the importance of political reconciliation and cooperation between Somalia's federal government, federal member states and other stakeholders. The leaders called for stronger relations through dialogue, good governance and peacebuilding to support security, stability and economic development. Their appeal comes as Somalia faces political disagreements over constitutional amendments, the mandates of federal institutions and the timetable for national elections. Opposition groups and the administrations of Puntland and Jubaland have rejected constitutional changes extending presidential and parliamentary terms, calling for a negotiated political settlement. The federal government maintains that the amendments provide a legal basis for elections scheduled in 2027. The joint communiqué did not announce any mediation initiative or specific agreement to resolve the political dispute. The two presidents also reviewed progress in bilateral economic cooperation, welcoming agreements and decisions reached during the Somalia-Uganda Joint Business Forum and Exhibition held in Mogadishu from Oct. 20 to 22. They welcomed the signing of a bilateral labor agreement and the agreed terms for a Bilateral Air Services Agreement aimed at expanding economic cooperation and transportation links. The leaders also revisited a proposal discussed during Hassan Sheikh's previous visit to Uganda on Oct. 26 to establish a warehouse in Mogadishu for Ugandan commercial goods. They agreed to continue considering the development of a port facility to facilitate trade and investment between the two countries. The proposals are intended to improve the movement of goods and expand commercial opportunities as Somalia and Uganda strengthen their economic partnership. Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to regional integration through the East African Community, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa and the African Union. They also called on international partners to continue supporting Somalia's security institutions, humanitarian response and efforts to address climate change. The presidents welcomed logistical and operational assistance provided by the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), which supports African Union peacekeeping operations and Somali security forces. At the conclusion of the visit, Hassan Sheikh invited Museveni to visit Somalia. The Ugandan president accepted the invitation, with the dates to be arranged through diplomatic channels. The joint communiqué was signed in Entebbe by Somalia's Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali and Ugandan Foreign Minister Adonia Ayebare. somalia.summary: Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni have agreed to enhance military cooperation against the al-Shabab militant group during a recent meeting in Entebbe, Uganda. They emphasized the need for intensified military operations and sustainable funding for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), especially as Uganda begins a phased withdrawal of its troops. The leaders called for increased offensive actions by AUSSOM and the Somali National Armed Forces while exploring alternative financing for military operations. They also highlighted the importance of political reconciliation within Somalia amid ongoing disputes over constitutional amendments and election timelines. Additionally, the two presidents discussed strengthening economic ties, including a bilateral labor agreement and potential trade facilitation projects. They reaffirmed their commitment to regional integration and called for continued international support for Somalia's security and humanitarian efforts. The meeting concluded with an invitation for Museveni to visit Somalia, which he accepted. (158 words)

somalia.title: Somalia announces killing of 285 al-Shabab fighters, including founding commanders - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia announces killing of 285 al-Shabab fighters, including founding commanders - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia announces killing of 285 al-Shabab fighters, including founding commanders Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 24, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali government announced on Monday that its forces killed 285 al-Shabab militants, including 12 senior commanders, during military operations across four regions in southern and central Somalia in recent weeks. Speaking at a news conference in Mogadishu on Nov. 23, outgoing Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi said the operations targeted senior al-Shabab figures, including founding members of the group and commanders responsible for military operations, communications, logistics and intelligence. advertisements The operations took place in Bay, Middle Shabelle, Lower Shabelle and Hiiraan regions, with some of the most significant fighting reported around Daynuunay in Bay region, according to the government. Fiqi said the operations were carried out by Somali National Army units, including Danab special forces, with air support from international partners. Among those reportedly killed was Isaaq Adan Madgaab, also known as Isaaq Ukurow, whom Fiqi described as one of the founding members of al-Shabab in 2007. “Ukurow had commanded a specialized unit responsible for carrying out attacks and had previously overseen six battalions operating in Bay and Bakool regions,” the minister said. According to Fiqi, Ukurow was killed during operations in the Daynuunay area. The minister also identified Mukhtaar Qalinle, known as Timo-weyne, as the group's communications chief, and Hassan Dheere as the commander responsible for central logistics and transportation. Both were reportedly killed during the Daynuunay operations. Other commanders named by Fiqi included Ahmed Abdulle Ansaari, who headed an al-Shabab unit operating in Middle Shabelle and was reportedly killed near Masjid Ali Gaduud. Mohamed Ibrahim Saadaat, described as a combat commander, was reportedly killed in the Muduulow area of Lower Shabelle. The minister also named Abdiwahab, known as Nuux-yare, whom he identified as an intelligence commander, and Abdullahi Ahmed Adan, also known as Maskiinow, a senior figure in the group's central logistics operations. Abdi Ali, whom Fiqi described as al-Shabab's governor for the Nuur Dugle area, was also among those reportedly killed. Another senior figure identified by the minister was Said Ahmed Sabriye Gaagaale, whom he described as one of the group's founding commanders and head of its heavy weapons and combat vehicles unit. Fiqi said Gaagaale was killed during an operation in Middle Shabelle region. The government did not provide a detailed breakdown of the reported casualties by location or disclose whether Somali forces suffered losses during the operations. The casualty figures and the identities and roles of the commanders reportedly killed could not be independently verified. Al-Shabab had not publicly commented on the government's latest claims. Fiqi said the objective of the operations was not merely to report battlefield casualties but to create conditions in which civilians could return to their normal lives. He emphasized that military success should be measured by whether children could attend school safely, traders could conduct business without fear and farmers could return to their fields. The minister also praised Somali troops involved in the operations and thanked international partners for supporting the military campaign, particularly through air operations. His announcement came on the same day Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre appointed Saadaq Omar Mohamed Hassan, widely known as Saadaq Joon, as the country's new defence minister. The government did not announce any changes to the ongoing military operations following the Cabinet reshuffle. Somali forces have been conducting offensives against al-Shabab in several parts of southern and central Somalia as the country prepares to assume greater security responsibilities from African Union peacekeeping troops. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-affiliated militant group, has waged an insurgency against Somalia's federal government for nearly two decades and continues to carry out attacks despite sustained military operations.
